newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel may have to rethink fiscal policy -official.
newsitem.headline: Israel may have to rethink fiscal policy -official.

text.p: The head of the Treasury's budget division said on Sunday Israel might have to reconsider fiscal policy if the budget deficit continues to rise.
Ron Croll told reporters the Treasury would wait for figures from February and March before deciding on a cut in spending.
"In the event that we're still on a deficit track, it is possible to cut between 1.5 and two billion shekels. I think if we need a bigger cut we will have to reconsider our fiscal policy," he said.
He refused to say where the cuts would be made or how fiscal policy might be altered.
The government's budget deficit reached 1.28 billion shekels in January, prompting concern among Treasury officials and criticism over the goverment's method of projecting tax revenues.
"We have stumbled and failed," Treasury director-general David Brodet said in in a newspaper interview published on Friday.

"Our tax model on which we base our projections is too old, insensitive to the deep changes in the Israeli economy since the early 1990s. Since then the economy grew 50 percent," he told Yedioth Ahronoth.
Israel's 1997 budget calls for a deficit of 9.7 billion shekels, or 2.8 percent of gross domestic product. But the January figures and early figures for February cast doubt on meeting the target.

Croll said the size of the deficit would no doubt be influenced by the Bank of Israel's monetary policy and called on the bank to lower interest rates. The central bank is scheduled to announce its March monetary programme on Monday.
"I suggest that first of all Bank of Israel make a strategic decision to...lower the real interest rates until the monetary markets are balanced," Croll said.
He said he would like to see the base rate, now at 14.2 percent, lowered immediately by up to 1.25 percentage points.
